blocks.text: Two main approaches for solving RL problems
Policy based method

Control, action, command, policy, input, stimuli, actuation refer to the same thing with sometime a slightly different meaning. Therefore, this is better to give a formal definition. A policy π is a map from state to action. What is the meaning of policy in the context of PID control? What is the meaning of policy in the context of some optimization based control? Policy-based methods learn this policy π. The policy can also be defined as a probability distribution over the set of actions, which is represented as π (a ∣ s).
blocks.heading: Policy based method

blocks.text: Value based method

Suppose you want to be a rich person, so marrying a rich person can also be an option. Bank robbery can also be an option if it is legal but it has more risk. In value based method, the agent learns the value of states which are close to goal. For example, the state achieved by a bank robbery (action) may not have good value. The value of a state under a policy π is given by V π (s) = E π [R t+1 + γ R t+2 + … ∣ s t =s]. Example Q learning

blocks.text: Initialize a Q -table with zeros

This q-table has 20 × 20 × 3 = 1200 values. Consider it like a look-up table. Our mountain car is in one of the 400 states and we will check which one of the three actions is good for it according to the table that we have. We can also randomly initialized this table. Assume that there exists some ideal table, which we can use to reach the flag. Since we do not have such table, we use Q -learning to learn that table. Q -learning is about learning Q-table.
blocks.heading: Initialize a Q -table with zeros

blocks.text: How to learn your Q-table

The procedure is somewhat same as you learnt weights of a neural network but there is one difference that we do not have labelled data pairs. Our agent will interact with the environment and learn through experience. Learning through experience is called Reinforcement Learning. The agent is exactly like you, students! You came to IIT and were looking for tasty options of food. You tried in different restaurants. Initially, you explored more. You started visiting your favourite restaurants untill you found the better one through exploration. This is called exploration-exploitation trade-off. In summary, you initialize the Q-table randomly and update it as you get more and more experience.
blocks.heading: How to learn your Q-table

blocks.text: Our Q-agent has a few more similarities with you!

Each semester you say, let me explore new opportunities in campus (make new friends, participate in student gymkhana, sleep, play games, skip lectures, etc.) and I will study the next semester onwards. If studying is an optimal policy π ∗, so value of a state s under the optimal policy π ∗ will be the optimal value V ∗ π (s). In current semester, your state is s t, you take action a t and you reach to a new state s t+1 in the next semester. The reward of the current semester will be printed in your transcript in golden colors is R t+1 = r(s t, a t). Here r is a function that assigns a real value to each state-action pair. So your Q-table for each (s t, a t) pair will look like Q π ∗ (s t, a t) = r(s t, a t) + γ V π ∗ (s t+1) From the next semester onwards, you are planning to take the optimal policy π ∗, which is the best among all possible policies. If you have chosen a t which maximizes your Q-value, you will get optimal V-value as well. V ∗ (s t) = max a Q π ∗ (s t, a).
blocks.heading: Our Q-agent has a few more similarities with you!

blocks.text: The update rule for the Q-agent

The update rule of Q function is inspired by the stochastic approximation technique that we discused in the class. It is very much intuitional as you can see below: Q new (s,a) = (1- α) Q old (s,a) + α × update term, where α ∈ ]0,1[ is called learning rate. α = 0: do not change or learn α = 1: forget everything about past
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q-agent

blocks.text: Several different algorithms are developed by defining the update term differently. The update term is R t+1 + γ V ∗ (s t+1), here γ ∈ ]0,1[ is a discount factor. The choice of the discount factor helps you to get a balance between your current reward and future Q-function.
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q-agent

blocks.text: Therefore,
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q-agent

blocks.text: Q new (s t,a t) = (1- α) Q old (s t,a t) + α (R t+1 + γ V ∗ (s t+1)), which is the same as
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q-agent

blocks.text: Q new (s t,a t) = Q old (s t,a t) + α (R t+1 + γ V ∗ (s t+1) - Q old (s t,a t)),
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q-agent

blocks.text: We can write the code to update the Q table:
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q-agent

blocks.text: q[state p, state v, action] = q[state p, state v, action] + learning rate a (reward + discount factor g np.max(q[new state p, new state v,:]) - q[state p, state v, action]
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q-agent

Control, action, command, policy, input, stimuli, actuation refer to the same thing with sometime a slightly different meaning. Therefore, this is better to give a formal definition. Suppose you want to be a rich person, so marrying a rich person can also be an option. Bank robbery can also be an option if it is legal but it has more risk. blocks.text: Initialize a Q -table with zeros

This q-table has 20 × 20 × 3 = 1200 values. Consider it like a look-up table. Our mountain car is in one of the 400 states and we will check which one of the three actions is good for it according to the table that we have. We can also randomly initialized this table. Assume that there exists some ideal table, which we can use to reach the flag. Since we do not have such table, we use Q -learning to learn that table. Q -learning is about learning Q-table.

blocks.text: How to learn your Q-table

The procedure is somewhat same as you learnt weights of a neural network but there is one difference that we do not have labelled data pairs. Our agent will interact with the environment and learn through experience. Learning through experience is called Reinforcement Learning. The agent is exactly like you, students! You came to IIT and were looking for tasty options of food. You tried in different restaurants. Initially, you explored more. You started visiting your favourite restaurants untill you found the better one through exploration. This is called exploration-exploitation trade-off. In summary, you initialize the Q-table randomly and update it as you get more and more experience.
blocks.heading: How to learn your Q-table

blocks.text: Our Q-agent has a few more similarities with you!

Each semester you say, let me explore new opportunities in campus (make new friends, participate in student gymkhana, sleep, play games, skip lectures, etc.) and I will study the next semester onwards. If studying is an optimal policy π ∗, so value of a state s under the optimal policy π ∗ will be the optimal value V ∗ π (s). In current semester, your state is s t, you take action a t and you reach to a new state s t+1 in the next semester. The reward of the current semester will be printed in your transcript in golden colors is R t+1 = r(s t, a t). Here r is a function that assigns a real value to each state-action pair. So your Q-table for each (s t, a t) pair will look like Q π ∗ (s t, a t) = r(s t, a t) + γ V π ∗ (s t+1) From the next semester onwards, you are planning to take the optimal policy π ∗, which is the best among all possible policies. If you have chosen a t which maximizes your Q-value, you will get optimal V-value as well. V ∗ (s t) = max a Q π ∗ (s t, a).
blocks.heading: Our Q-agent has a few more similarities with you!

blocks.text: The update rule for the Q-agent

The update rule of Q function is inspired by the stochastic approximation technique that we discused in the class. It is very much intuitional as you can see below: Q new (s,a) = (1- α) Q old (s,a) + α × update term, where α ∈ ]0,1[ is called learning rate. α = 0: do not change or learn α = 1: forget everything about past
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q-agent

blocks.text: Several different algorithms are developed by defining the update term differently. The update term is R t+1 + γ V ∗ (s t+1), here γ ∈ ]0,1[ is a discount factor. The choice of the discount factor helps you to get a balance between your current reward and future Q-function.
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q-agent

blocks.text: Therefore,
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q-agent

blocks.text: Q new (s t,a t) = (1- α) Q old (s t,a t) + α (R t+1 + γ V ∗ (s t+1)), which is the same as
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q-agent

blocks.text: Q new (s t,a t) = Q old (s t,a t) + α (R t+1 + γ V ∗ (s t+1) - Q old (s t,a t)),
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q-agent

blocks.text: We can write the code to update the Q table:
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q-agent

blocks.text: q[state p, state v, action] = q[state p, state v, action] + learning rate a (reward + discount factor g np.max(q[new state p, new state v,:]) - q[state p, state v, action]

1. Problem Formulation: Sutton & Barto Example 4.3 (Gambler's Problem)

A gambler has the opportunity to make bets on the outcomes of a sequence of coin flips: If the coin lands heads, the gambler wins as many dollars as staked on that flip. If the coin lands tails, the gambler loses the stake. The game terminates when the gambler either reaches the goal of 100, or loses all money (0 capital). On each flip, the gambler decides what integer stake a to wager, where a ∈ {1, 2, …, min (s, 100 - s)} and s is the current capital.

blocks.text: Markov Decision Process (MDP) Formulation:

State Space (S): Current capital in integer dollars: S = {1, 2, …, 99} Terminal States (S +): S + = {0, 100} with boundary conditions V(0) = 0 (ruin) and V(100) = 1 (goal) Action Space (A (s)): Permissible stakes given current capital s: A (s) = {1, 2, …, min (s, 100 - s)} since we have a ≤ s, a ≤ 100-s. Figure 4.3 from Sutton & Barto (Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd Edition, page 84) illustrates two key RL concepts:
blocks.heading: 4. Visualization Sutton & Barto Figure 4.3

blocks.text: Value Function Sweeps (Top Panel): In early sweeps (k=1, 2, 3), non-terminal values remain zero except at states from which the goal (100) can be reached within k flips. Values propagate backwards from the absorbing goal s=100, forming distinctive step plateaus at binary powers (50, 75, 25, …). As k → ∞, V(s) smoothly approaches the optimal probability of winning the game from capital s. Optimal Policy Structure (Bottom Panel): The optimal policy exhibits a famous sawtooth / pyramidal structure with major peaks at s=25, 50, 75, and sub-peaks at 12, 37, 62, 87. Why does the policy stake 50 at 50? Because the coin flip is unfavorable (p h = 0.4 < 0.5). In any unfavorable game, the law of large numbers works against the gambler with every additional flip. Thus, the optimal approach is bold play: make the fewest possible bets to reach the goal! At s=50, staking 50 gives a direct 40\% chance of reaching 100 in just one flip. Betting smaller stakes would require winning multiple coin tosses, where (0.4) n diminishes exponentially. Multiplicity of Optimal Policies: There are numerous ties in Q (s, a). For example, at capital s=50, staking 50 or staking 25 can lead to equivalent expected values if followed by optimal play. Picking the first maximizer (smallest stake) yields the classic plot published in the book.

blocks.text: Terms Term Meaning --- --- Player The agent (us). Plays against the dealer. Dealer The opponent. Follows a fixed rule (part of the environment). Card sum Total value of the cards in a hand. Face cards Jack, Queen, King. Each counts as 10. Ace Counts as either 1 or 11. Usable ace An ace that can count as 11 without the sum going over 21. Dealer's showing card The dealer's one face-up card (the other is hidden). Hit Ask for one more card. Stick Stop taking cards; the turn ends. Bust Card sum goes over 21. The hand loses immediately. Natural 21 with the first two cards (an ace + a 10-valued card). Infinite deck Cards are drawn with replacement, so past cards give no information.
blocks.heading: 1. Blackjack (Sutton & Barto, Example 5.1)

blocks.text: Rules Player and dealer each get 2 cards. One dealer card is face up. Natural: if the player has a natural, they win, unless the dealer also has one (then it is a draw). Player's turn: hit or stick repeatedly. If the player goes bust, they lose. Dealer's turn: the dealer hits until their sum is 17 or more, then sticks. If the dealer goes bust, the player wins. Otherwise, the sum closer to 21 wins; equal sums are a draw. Reward at the end of the game: +1 win, 0 draw, −1 lose.

blocks.text: 3. First-Visit Monte Carlo Prediction
Idea: v π (s) is an expected return, so estimate it by averaging the returns seen after visiting s: V(s) = frac 1 N(s) Σ i=1 N(s) G i(s) longrightarrow v π (s) as N(s) → ∞
blocks.heading: 3. First-Visit Monte Carlo Prediction

blocks.text: Here, N(s) is the number of episodes so far in which state s was visited (counting only the first visit in each episode), and G i(s) is the return that followed the i -th of these visits.
blocks.heading: 3. First-Visit Monte Carlo Prediction

blocks.text: Instead of storing all returns, use the incremental mean: N(S t) ← N(S t) + 1, V(S t) ← V(S t) + frac 1 N(S t) [ G - V(S t) ]
blocks.heading: 3. First-Visit Monte Carlo Prediction

Policy based method

Control, action, command, policy, input, stimuli, actuation refer to the same thing with sometime a slightly different meaning. Therefore, this is better to give a formal definition. A policy π is a map from state to action. What is the meaning of policy in the context of PID control? What is the meaning of policy in the context of some optimization based control? blocks.text: Value based method

Suppose you want to be a rich person, so marrying a rich person can also be an option. Bank robbery can also be an option if it is legal but it has more risk. In value based method, the agent learns the value of states which are close to goal. For example, the state achieved by a bank robbery (action) may not have good value. The value of a state under a policy π is given by V π (s) = E π [R t+1 + γ R t+2 + … ∣ s t =s]. Example Q learning

blocks.text: How to learn your Q -table

The procedure is somewhat same as you learnt weights of a neural network but there is one difference that we do not have labelled data pairs. Our agent will interact with the environment and learn through experience. Learning through experience is called Reinforcement Learning. The agent is exactly like you, students! You came to IIT and were looking for tasty options of food. You tried in different restaurants. Initially, you explored more. You started visiting your favourite restaurants untill you found the better one through exploration. This is called exploration-exploitation trade-off. In summary, you initialize the Q -table randomly and update it as you get more and more experience.
blocks.heading: How to learn your Q -table

blocks.text: Our Q -agent has a few more similarities with you!

Each semester you say, let me explore new opportunities in campus (make new friends, participate in student gymkhana, sleep, play games, skip lectures, etc.) and I will study the next semester onwards. If studying is an optimal policy π ∗, so value of a state s under the optimal policy π ∗ will be the optimal value V ∗ π (s). In current semester, your state is s t, you take action a t and you reach to a new state s t+1 in the next semester. The reward of the current semester will be printed in your transcript in golden colors is R t+1 = r(s t, a t). Here r is a function that assigns a real value to each state-action pair. So your Q-table for each (s t, a t) pair will look like Q π ∗ (s t, a t) = r(s t, a t) + γ V π ∗ (s t+1) From the next semester onwards, you are planning to take the optimal policy π ∗, which is the best among all possible policies. If you have chosen a t which maximizes your Q-value, you will get optimal V-value as well. V ∗ (s t) = max a Q π ∗ (s t, a).

blocks.text: The update rule for the Q -agent

The update rule of Q function is inspired by the stochastic approximation technique that we discused in the class. It is very much intuitional as you can see below: Q new (s,a) = (1- α) Q old (s,a) + α × update term, where α ∈ (0,1) is called learning rate. α = 0: do not change or learn α = 1: forget everything about past
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q -agent

blocks.text: Several different algorithms are developed by defining the update term differently. The update term is R t+1 + γ V ∗ (s t+1), here γ ∈ (0,1) is a discount factor. The choice of the discount factor helps you to get a balance between your current reward and future Q -function.
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q -agent

blocks.text: Therefore,
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q -agent

blocks.text: Q new (s t,a t) = (1- α) Q old (s t,a t) + α (R t+1 + γ V ∗ (s t+1)), which is the same as
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q -agent

blocks.text: Q new (s t,a t) = Q old (s t,a t) + α (R t+1 + γ V ∗ (s t+1) - Q old (s t,a t)),
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q -agent

blocks.text: We can write the code to update the Q table:
blocks.heading: The update rule for the Q -agent

blocks.text: q[state p, state v, action] = q[state p, state v, action] + learning rate a (reward + discount factor g np.max(q[new state p, new state v,:]) - q[state p, state v, action]

In this tutorial, we transition to Deep Q-Networks (DQN) , replacing the lookup table with a deep neural network function approximator to control the continuous-state of CartPole-v1 .

1. Motivation: From Tabular Q-Learning to Deep Q-Networks
In Tutorial 3, we solved MountainCar-v0 by discretizing continuous position and velocity into a 20 × 20 × 3 lookup table:
Q(s t, a t) ← Q(s t, a t) + α [ R t+1 + γ max a' Q(s t+1, a') - Q(s t, a t) ]
Why Move from a Table to a Neural Network?

No Manual Discretization: Instead of hand-crafting arbitrary bin boundaries, a neural network Q(s, a; θ) ≈ Q (s, a) accepts continuous states directly (such as cart position, cart velocity, pole angle, and angular velocity). Generalization: Learning in one state smoothly updates network weights, improving value estimates for nearby unvisited states. Scalability: Tabular methods explode exponentially in higher-dimensional robotics, while neural networks scale to complex continuous spaces.
blocks.heading: Why Move from a Table to a Neural Network?

blocks.text: DeepMind's Two Core Stabilizations (2015)

Experience Replay: Stores transitions (s, a, r, s', d) in a buffer and samples random mini-batches → breaks temporal correlation and restores i.i.d. training. Target Network (Q target): A slowly updated network copy used to compute Bellman bootstrap targets → eliminates the "moving target" problem.

blocks.text: ε -Greedy Policy: Balances exploration (random action with probability ε) and exploitation (greedy action argmax a Q with probability 1 - ε). ε decays from 1.0 down to 0.05. Soft Target Update (Polyak Averaging): Slowly tracks the online network at every step: θ target ← τ θ online + (1 - τ) θ target (τ = 0.005)
